pages.content:
- In C++, a string is a sequence of characters. Strings are widely used for handling text data such as names, messages, and input/output operations.
Example: "Hello" – This is a string.

- To use strings, we need to include the `` header file. While including `` already covers it in most cases, it is still good practice to explicitly include `` when using string functions.

---

**Declaring a String:**
```cpp
string message; // Declaring a string variable without initializing
```
 **Initializing a String:**
```cpp
message = "Hello, World!"; // Initializing the string with a value
```

Alternatively, declare and initialize in a single step:
```cpp
string greeting = "Hello, World!"; // Declaring and initializing in one step
```

pages.title: String Length and Empty Check
pages.content:
In C++, strings are objects that represent sequences of characters. Now we'll explore two important methods for working with strings: length() (or size()) and empty().

---

**1. `length()` or `size()`**

These methods are used to find out how many characters are in a string. Both length() and size() return the same value and can be used interchangeably.


**Syntax**
```cpp
string_variable.length();
string_variable.size();
```

---

 **2. `empty()`**

This method checks if a string is empty (contains no characters). It returns a boolean value: `true` if the string is empty (i.e., contains zero characters), otherwise `false`.


**Syntax**
```cpp
string_variable.empty();
```

---

**Example Code**
```cpp
#include 
using namespace std;

int main() {
    string str = "Chocolate";  // Create a string with the word "Chocolate"

    cout << str.length() << endl;  // Print how many letters are in the word
    cout << str.empty() << endl;   // Print 1 if empty, 0 if not

    return 0;
}
```
**Expected Output**
```default
9  
0
```

pages.title: Finding Characters/Substrings using find() and rfind()
pages.content:
In C++, the `string` class provides the **`find()`** and **`rfind()`** methods to locate characters or substrings within a string. And returns `string::npos` if not found.

`std::npos` is a constant value of type `size_t` that represents the largest possible value for an index, typically used to indicate that a string or substring was not found in a search operation.

---

 **1. `find()`**

It searches for a character or substring within a string **from left to right** (beginning to end), and returns the **index of the first occurrence**. 

**Syntax:**
```cpp
string_variable.find();
```

---

**2. `rfind()`**

It searches for a character or substring within a string **from right to left** (end to beginning) and returns the **index of the last occurrence**.

**Syntax:**
```cpp
string_variable.rfind();
```

---

**Example:**
```cpp
#include 
using namespace std;;

int main() {
    string text = "online";          // A simple word

    size_t first = text.find('n');   // Find first 'n'
    size_t last = text.rfind('n');   // Find last 'n'

    cout << first << endl;           // Show first 'n' position Output: 1
    cout << last << endl;            // Show last 'n' position Output: 4

    return 0;
}
```

pages.title: string append() method
pages.content:
In C++, the `append()` method is a function used with the `string` class to add one string to the end of another. It is often used when working with text data like names, messages, or combining user input. To use strings and the `append()` method, the `` header must be included.

**Syntax:**
```cpp
string1.append(string2);
```

---

**Example:**
```cpp
#include    // For input and output
using namespace std;

int main() {
    string str1 = "Hello, ";   // First string
    string str2 = "World!";    // Second string
    str1.append(str2);         // Append str2 to str1
    cout << str1 << endl;      // Print the final result
    return 0;                  // End of program
}
```
**Expected Output:**


pages.title: transform() with toupper in C++
pages.content:
In C++, `transform()` is used with `::toupper` to convert all characters in a string to uppercase.
This method is very useful when formatting text or preparing strings for case-insensitive comparisons. To use this feature, the `` and `` headers must be included.

**Syntax:**
```cpp
// The transform function is used to apply a transformation to each element in a range
transform(
    str.begin(),  // The beginning of the range (start of the string)
    str.end(),    // The end of the range (end of the string)
    str.begin(),  // The destination where transformed elements are stored (same string)
    ::toupper     // The transformation applied to each element (convert to uppercase)
);
```

---

**Example:**
```cpp
#include      // For input and output
#include     // For transform

using namespace std;

int main() {
    string str = "coding is fun";   // Original string
    transform(str.begin(), str.end(), str.begin(), ::toupper); // Convert to uppercase
    cout << "Uppercase String: " << str << endl;  // Display result
    return 0;  // End of program
}
```
**Expected Output:**
```default
Uppercase String: CODING IS FUN
```

This technique is useful for normalizing input, performing case-insensitive comparisons, or simply formatting text consistently. To utilize this feature, the `` and `` headers must be included.

**Syntax:**
```cpp
#include   // For transform

transform(
    str.begin(),    // Start of the string
    str.end(),      // End of the string
    str.begin(),    // Destination (same string)
    ::tolower       // Function applied to each character (convert to lowercase)
);
```

---

**Example:**
```cpp
#include      // For input and output
#include     // For transform

using namespace std;

int main() {
    string str = "C++ Programming Is Powerful!";  // Original string

    cout << "Lowercase String: " << str << endl;  // Display result
    return 0;  // End of program
}
```

```default
Lowercase String: c++ programming is powerful!
```

In C++, the `insert()` method is used to add characters or substrings at a specific position in a string.
This method is useful when you want to **insert text without replacing existing content**—such as adding a middle name, inserting punctuation, or dynamically modifying strings during input processing.

To use the `insert()` method, the `` header must be included.

```cpp
stringName.insert(position, "textToInsert");
// position: the index at which to insert new text
```

```cpp
#include      // For input and output
using namespace std;

int main() {
    string fullName = "John Doe";                // Original string
    fullName.insert(5, "Michael ");              // Insert "Michael " after "John "
    cout << "Updated Full Name: " << fullName << endl;  // Display result
    return 0;  // End of program
}
```

pages.title: stoi() and stof() in C++
pages.content:
In C++, `stoi()` and `stof()` are used to convert strings to numeric values.
These functions are especially useful when reading input as strings (e.g., from a file or user input) and converting that data into numeric types for calculations or logic.
- `stoi()` converts a string to an `int`.
- `stof()` converts a string to a `float`.

These functions are part of the `` library.

**Syntax:**
```cpp
int number = stoi(stringValue);   // Convert string to int
float decimal = stof(stringValue); // Convert string to float
```

---

**Example:**
```cpp
#include      // For input and output
using namespace std;

int main() {
    string intString = "42";      // String representing an integer
    string floatString = "3.14";  // String representing a float

    int number = stoi(intString);     // Convert to int
    float decimal = stof(floatString); // Convert to float

    cout << "Integer: " << number << endl;
    cout << "Float: " << decimal << endl;

    return 0;  // End of program
}
```
**Expected Output:**
```default 
Integer: 42  
Float: 3.14
```

pages.title: to_string() conversion in C++
pages.content:
In C++, converting numbers and other data types to `string` is essential for tasks like formatting output, displaying values, or preparing data for storage and transmission.
The `to_string()` function is a convenient built-in method used to convert numeric values such as `int`, `float`, and `double` into their string representations.

To use `to_string()`, the  header must be included.

**Syntax:**
```cpp
string strValue = to_string(value);  
// Converts value (int, float, double, etc.) to a string
```

---

**Examples:**
```cpp
#include      // For input and output
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int intValue = 42;                  // Integer value
    float floatValue = 3.14159;         // Float value
    double doubleValue = 2.718281;      // Double value

    string intString = to_string(intValue);         // Convert int to string
    string floatString = to_string(floatValue);     // Convert float to string
    string doubleString = to_string(doubleValue);   // Convert double to string

    cout << "Integer as string: " << intString << endl;
    cout << "Float as string: " << floatString << endl;
    cout << "Double as string: " << doubleString << endl;

    return 0;  // End of program
}
```
**Expected Output:**
```default
Integer as string: 42
Float as string: 3.141590
Double as string: 2.718281
```

practiceProblems.description:
**Strings**  are used for storing text.

A  **string**  variable contains a collection of characters surrounded by double quotes. Before declaring a variable as  string  the  `string datatype` must be used.

For example:
```cpp
string name = "Chef";
```

We print string like we print any other variable.
```cpp
string name = "Chef";
cout << name;
```
 
### Task
Write a program which does the following
- Declare a string variable named `fruit` and assign the value "Apple" to it.
- Output the value stored in `fruit` to the console.

practiceProblems.description:
C++ uses the **+** sign for both  `addition`  and  `concatenation`.
- Numbers are added. 
- `Strings`  are concatenated. 
- We cannot mix the two.

### Task
You are given a program in the IDE:
- You want to output **2569**.
- Try running the given code in the IDE as it is - it will give a  **`Compilation error`**.
- Fix the error so that both the  `variables`  become  **`string`** and the output is **2569**.

practiceProblems.title: Printing Characters From a String
practiceProblems.description:
We can access the characters in a  `string`  by referring to its  `index number`  inside square brackets **[ ]**.\
We use the concept of indexing which means every character in a  `string`  corresponds to a number called the `index number`.  

![index](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/string_index_numbers.png)

 
**Note:** 
- `Indexing`  always starts from $0$ when going left to right. 
- So the first character of a `string` **s** is **s[0]**, the second is **s[1]**, and so on.

### Task
- Update the given code in IDE to print the characters **o** and **r** (with a space between them) from the string using indexing.

practiceProblems.title: Changing Characters in a String
practiceProblems.description:
To change the value of a specific character in a  string
- We refer to the index number to access the specific character by using the indexing operator **`[]`**
- We then assign the new character (enclosed in single quotes ' ' ) to it.

For example
```cpp
string myString = "Chaf";
myString[2] = 'e';

cout << myString;

// Output:
// Chef
```

Here we changed the character at index 2 of "Chaf" which is 'a' with 'e'. Remember indexing always starts from 0.


### Task
Write a program which does the following
- Initialise a  string variable  **`word`**  and assign the value  "Ocygen"  to it.
- You now want to fix the typo in the given  `string`.
- Use the syntax explained above to replace  `'c'`  with  `'x'`  in the variable  **`word`**
- Output the updated  **`word`**  to console

practiceProblems.title: Substring
practiceProblems.description:
A substring is a small part of a string.  
For example:  
"World" is a substring of the string "Hello World!"  
In C++, the `substr()` is a string function which is used to extract a substring from a given string.  

We takes two values:
- the starting index of the substring
- the number of characters in the substring
```cpp
string str = "Hello, World!";
cout<<str.substr(7, 5);
```
This outputs 
```cpp
World
```
It goes to the seventh index which is 'W' and takes 5 characters starting from 'W', which results in 'World'.   
We can even give only the starting index to the substr function.  
In that case it will start from the starting index and go till the end of the string.
```cpp
string str = "Hello, World!";
cout<<str.substr(5);
```
This outputs
```cpp
, World!
```
as it starts from the fifth index which is ',' and goes till the end of the string. 

Please note that if we provide invalid starting index, the program will throw an error.
### Task
- Update the given code in IDE to print **fruit**.

pages.title: Introduction to the module on Strings
pages.content:
So far, we have focused on logic, integers, math. \
The module on logic building and problem solving primarily covered number operations. 

It is time to add 'Strings' to our arsenal for solving programming problems.

Lets revise some basic syntax of strings.
- Strings are a **datatype**.
  - A string is composed of characters. A single character can be any letter, any digit, symbol, etc.
  - A **binary string** is one which has only '0' and '1' as component characters
  - The character in the $i^{th}$ index of a string is represented as **S[i]**

Click in **Next** to proceed.

pages.title: Review problem - 1
pages.content:
Malvika likes only $2$ colours - amber and brass. \
Her mother bought $n$ balloons - each of which is either amber or brass in colour. \
The colours of the balls is provided as a string consisting of characters 'a' and 'b'
- 'a' denotes amber coloured balloon
- 'b' denotes brass coloured balloon

Malvika wants all balloons to be of the same colour - she can paint some balloons with opposite colour. \
Find out the **minimum** number of balloons she needs to paint to make all of them the same colour.
